newsitem.title: FRANCE: Shocked French right bickers over defeat.
newsitem.headline: Shocked French right bickers over defeat.

text.p: A shell-shocked French right erupted into bitter bickering after its election defeat on Sunday and several of its rival leaders thrust themselves forward to lead the long march back to power.

The ruling alliance of President Jacques Chirac's Gaullist RPR and the centrist UDF suffered a stunning defeat, four years after routing the left which has now been returned to power with an absolute majority in the National Assembly.
Calls for a profound overhaul of the conservative coalition came from both the RPR and the UDF, with senior politicians on both sides stepping forward to lead a reform.

The defeat was a stinging blow to Chirac, and former centrist president Valery Giscard d'Estaing quickly accused him of imprudence for calling the snap election despite his own unpopularity nearly 10 months ahead of schedule.
"I think that people took a big risk of a negative vote by deciding to ask French citizens when it was known they were unhappy with the way they were being governed," he said.
Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe has bowed out after taking the blame for the first-round election defeat.
Chirac's fellow-Gaullist rival for the presidency in 1995, ex-premier Edouard Balladur, said the defeat exposed the need for a deep review of the right's policies and organisation.
"Everything shows that the former majority is no longer representative of the schools of thought that make it up...We must review our political organisation and conceive a coherent message," he said.
"I intend to devote myself to a necessary re-foundation," echoed former hardline Gaullist interior minister Charles Pasqua who had backed Balladur against Chirac for the presidency.
National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, anointed last-ditch saviour last week after Juppe dropped out, made a direct bid for the leadership of the right.
He said he was utterly determined to prepare for a return to power "with all those who share the same conception of France, of France in Europe and to prepare for a different tomorrow".

Seguin, who led the "no" campaign in a 1992 referendum on the Maastricht Treaty on European union, was the main critic of Juppe's austerity policies geared to make France meet the criteria for joining the single European currency.
The UDF centrist umbrella group appeared to be on the verge of breaking up.
"We cannot go on like this," Education Minister Francois Bayrou said. "The organisation we had so far is dead."
Free-marketeer ex-finance minister Alain Madelin, who leads the UDF's liberal wing, announced he would found a new group.
"The page has been turned. I feel a free man," he said.
He said he would regroup his liberal friends to work for a return to power.
Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure had warned before the poll that a fiasco could blow the right to pieces.
A saying often attributed to the late president Charles de Gaulle is that France has "the world's most stupid right".
The conservatives were divided on whether Chirac was right to call the snap election, and on the policies the conservatives were proposing if they won.

Even before the election, the right was weakened by cracks between and within the RPR and its UDF junior partner. European policy was one issue of discord, with the UDF generally more pro-European than the RPR.
Juppe's policy divided the RPR between supporters of his Maastricht-inspired austerity policy, and those of Seguin who called for a more social approach to the single European currency.
The 1995 election which pitted Balladur against Chirac caused deep and lasting resentment.
The "balladuriens" were plunged into disgrace until their recent recall from the political wilderness because of the need to paper over the cracks and present a united election front.
